references.text: John had previously been questioned about his role and ministry, including the question of why he baptized. This background sheds light on the discussion that arises in John 3:25 concerning purification and baptism ([ref:Joh 1:25-28|John 1:25-28]).

The water jars mentioned at the wedding in Cana were set out "as the Jewish custom of purification required" ([ref:Joh 2:6|John 2:6]). This shows the Jewish context for purification (καθαρισμός) that is the subject of the discussion in John 3:25.

The immediate context: Jesus and his disciples were baptizing in Judea, while John was baptizing at Aenon. This parallel baptismal activity forms the background for the dispute over purification ([ref:Joh 3:22-23|John 3:22-23]).
The dispute over purification leads to John's disciples coming to him with concern that Jesus is also baptizing and that "all" are going to him ([ref:Joh 3:26|John 3:26]).

The tension between the baptismal activities of John and Jesus is further confirmed here, where it is mentioned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was gaining more disciples and baptizing more than John ([ref:Joh 4:1-2|John 4:1-2]).

The Pharisees and scribes confronted Jesus with questions about purification and Jewish purity laws. The question of καθαρισμός (purification) was a central point of contention in Jewish practice ([ref:Mark 7:1-4|Mark 7:1-4]).
The Old Testament basis for water purification is found in the Mosaic Law, where water cleansing was prescribed ([ref:3 Mos 15:13|Leviticus 15:13]).

The purification rituals in the Mosaic Law, such as cleansing with water, form the background for the Jewish discussion about purification (καθαρισμός) that John's disciples were involved in ([ref:4 Mos 19:7|Numbers 19:7]).

God's promise to sprinkle clean water and cleanse his people points to the eschatological expectation of purification that may have underlain the discussion about purification in John 3:25 ([ref:Esek 36:25|Ezekiel 36:25]).
